content_html:
Biological and physical memories

Biological memories beyond the brain - immune “trained immunity” and epigenetic cell memory show durable, experience-dependent changes outside neural tissue.

Trained immunity shows that even innate immune cells (monocytes, NK cells) can undergo long-lasting changes after infection or vaccination. Traditionally, only adaptive immunity (T/B cells) was thought to have memory. The mechanism inviolves exposure to a pathogen or stimulus → epigenetic reprogramming (histone modifications, chromatin accessibility) → heightened or altered response to later challenges. Example: BCG vaccination not only protects against tuberculosis but also enhances general resistance to unrelated infections.

Epigenetic Cell Memory describes how cells carry molecular memories of past signals via stable changes in gene regulation. Mechanisms include DNA methylation, Histone modifications, Chromatin structure changes. These can persist through cell divisions, effectively “remembering” environmental exposures (nutrition, toxins, stress). For example, plants show stress memory across generations; in humans, early famine exposure can alter descendants’ metabolic risk.

Memory is not confined to the brain - it is a general biological principle of persistence and plasticity. Trained immunity and epigenetic memory influence susceptibility to infections, autoimmunity, cancer, and ageing. Memory as “lasting modification of response potential” links neural, immune, and cellular domains.

How is memory carried to next generation?

Memory is, in a sense, retained through genetic inheritance (the DNA sequence itself is passed on through gametes (sperm/egg), which carries coded potential, but not experience) and through epigenetic inheritance (chemical marks on DNA or histones, or small RNAs, can also be transmitted; they don’t change the DNA code but affect how it is used).

Cross-Generational “Memory” happens in different organisms. Plants show strong transgenerational stress memory (heat, drought, pathogen attack), often because germline resets are weaker than in animals. C. elegans (worms) use small RNA pathways that can transmit viral resistance or nutritional states for dozens of generations. In mammals (humans, mice), most epigenetic marks are erased during gamete and embryo reprogramming, but some “escapees” persist, creating intergenerational or sometimes transgenerational effects. Small RNAs transmit viral defense, starvation, even neuronal experience, lasting multiple generations, but stronger resetting in mammals limits true transgenerational inheritance.

What is passed on is not “memory of events” but altered dispositions - metabolism, immune responsiveness, stress sensitivity. Neural memory which involves the recall of past experiences is not biologically heritable. Epigenetic memory however is potentially heritable, through the molecular persistence of past environments. Epigenetic inheritance lets organisms adapt to rapid environmental change without waiting for DNA mutations, for example, parental exposures (diet, toxins, stress) can increase or decrease disease risk in descendants.

In this sense, “memory” is expanded beyond the brain into a general principle of persistence, with echoes in both biology and culture.

Memory as state

“Memory” does not have to be biological or organic. In physics, chemistry, and materials science, there are many ways in which matter can “remember” past states. These are not conscious or neural memories, but they share the core property: an experience leaves a persistent trace that changes future behavior.

Magnetic materials “remember” their past exposure to magnetic fields (hysteresis). The magnetization curve depends on history, not just present input. Metals like Nitinol “remember” their pre-set shape and revert when heated. Metals retain traces of stresses (dislocation patterns) from previous loads. Amorphous solids (glasses) exhibit “aging” which reflects a memory of how they were cooled or stressed. Polymers & gels can encode stress/strain history in their internal microstructure.

On geological & planetary scales, tree rings, ice cores, and sediments have layers that physically store environmental history. Rock magnetization in basalt records Earth’s past magnetic field orientation.

Many systems can be seen as storing information about prior states (statistical mechanics, entropy). Dissipative structures are non-living systems (e.g., sand dunes, convection cells) that self-organize in ways that “record” boundary conditions. Utlimately the Universe can be seen as a memory substrate: the idea that information is never lost (linked to black hole physics) implies the cosmos itself retains traces of all interactions.

Non-organic “memory” is not about recall or awareness, but about state-dependence: the present configuration carries information about the past.

Physics of information

At its core, information is physical. That means it is not an abstract quantity floating outside matter and energy - it is embodied in the state of physical systems. This principle links information theory with statistical mechanics, thermodynamics, and quantum physics.

Information processing and thermodynamics are inseparable. Reducing uncertainty (gaining information) is like reducing entropy. Erasing one bit of information has a fundamental thermodynamic cost: computation is not free - information processing is bound by physical energy/heat.

The universe itself is an information-preserving system.

  • Information = physical state correlations.
  • Processing = physical transformations.
  • Memory = stable records of past states.

This unifies brains, DNA, computers, and even black holes under a shared informational physics. The physics of information shows that information is not abstract - it is inseparable from matter, energy, entropy, and the laws of physics.

Dissipative structures

Dissipative structures in non-living systems (e.g., sand dunes, convection cells) self-organize in ways that “record” boundary conditions. They are ordered patterns that form spontaneously in systems driven far from equilibrium. Introduced by Ilya Prigogine (Nobel Prize, 1977) as part of non-equilibrium thermodynamics, these structures require continuous energy or matter flow to be maintained. For example, with sand dunes & ripples, wind organizes grains into regular waveforms that reflect wind direction/speed. These structures arise because of external constraints (temperature gradient, wind speed, concentration). Their form encodes information about those conditions, and if conditions change, the structure reconfigures, retaining a trace of history until a new steady state is reached.

Dissipative structures illustrate how order can emerge from disorder through energy flow. They embody the principle that memory is not exclusive to living systems, but a general physical property of matter under constraints. This connects to broader ideas like the physics of information and non-organic memory.

While not “memory” in the neural sense, dissipative structures show persistence, sensitivity and record-keeping. Patterns remain as long as driving forces are present. Small differences in initial/boundary conditions → different emergent structures. Morphology serves as a record of past flows and constraints.

This parallels biological memory in that both are stable-yet-dynamic states that carry information from past inputs into future behavior. Dissipative structures are non-living systems that spontaneously self-organize under energy flow, creating patterns that act as physical records of their boundary conditions - a kind of non-organic “memory.” But at the same time, life itself can be considered a network of dissipative structures.

Universe as memory substrate

In physics, information is believed to be conserved - quantum unitarity says the full wavefunction evolves reversibly. If information can never be destroyed, then every interaction leaves a trace somewhere in the universe. This means the universe itself functions as a vast memory substrate: the present state implicitly encodes all past interactions.

Hawking radiation (1975) predicted that black holes radiate thermally and eventually evaporate, seemingly erasing information about what fell in, which clashes with quantum mechanics, which forbids information loss. The paradox spurred decades of debate: does the universe “forget” what falls into a black hole?

There** **may be a maximum amount of information (entropy) that can be stored in a given region, proportional to surface area not volume, and every bit of the universe’s state carries imprints of past dynamics. But though information is preserved microscopically, macroscopic entropy increase makes recovery practically impossible.

The universe “remembers” in a non-conscious, physical sense. Quantum correlations (entanglement) preserve histories, gravitational imprints (curvature, waves) carry records of events. Cosmic background radiation is a fossil record of the early universe. Thus, reality itself is a distributed ledger of all interactions - though inaccessible in practice.

This extends the idea of memory beyond organisms or devices to the fabric of spacetime itself. Memory here = no erasure of information, only redistribution and scrambling. The cosmos is an “infinite archive,” where nothing is truly lost, only hidden or transformed.

The holographic principle

The Holographic Principle is about the physics of Information on boundaries. The core idea is that all the information contained in a region of space can be described by degrees of freedom living on its boundary. It’s inspired by black hole physics: the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy of a black hole scales with the area of its event horizon, not the volume inside. Thus, the “storage capacity” of a region is proportional to its surface, like a hologram encoding a 3D image on a 2D surface.

It suggests that spacetime geometry itself emerges from patterns of entanglement - a deep informational view of reality. The universe may be fundamentally “2D” information living on cosmic boundaries, and geometry and gravity may arise from entanglement networks. Holography embodies the idea that the universe “remembers” by distributing information across surfaces.

This reframes reality as a cosmic memory compression algorithm: what seems volumetric is in fact encoded on surfaces. It unifies thermodynamics, quantum field theory, and gravity under information theory. The holographic principle says the universe’s memory is written not in volumes, but on boundaries - spacetime itself may be a hologram.

If information in a volume can be fully described by degrees of freedom on its boundary (bulk ↔ boundary duality), then the complexity of an organism (bulk) is encoded and constrained by simpler surface-level rules or representations (boundary). In evolution, boundaries are where organisms meet environment: membranes, skin, interfaces. These surfaces both encode environmental pressures and store adaptive history (e.g., protective pigmentation, immune receptors). The “boundary” reflects the evolutionary information of survival strategies, much like a holographic boundary encodes bulk physics.

Holography describes how volumetric complexity compresses to surface area. Evolution shows a similar drive: economy of coding (DNA encodes vast phenotypic variety with compact rules). Surface traits act as compressed signatures of deep evolutionary histories (camouflage patterns, mate signals, immune repertoires). In holography, entanglement structures build geometry; connectivity defines space; in evolution, ecological entanglements (predator–prey, host–symbiont, co-evolution) define the “geometry” of adaptive landscapes. The survival “space” of a species is determined less by isolated volume and more by relational links at boundaries.

No information is lost, it’s redistributed on surfaces. Even extinct lineages leave genomic echoes (pseudogenes, conserved motifs) and morphological traces in current organisms. The living surface of life (the biosphere) encodes the deep history of evolutionary bulk. Just as the holographic universe encodes bulk in boundary, evolution encodes life’s deep histories in interfaces and compressed surface traits. Both principles reveal a common theme: boundaries are not superficial - they are archives of complexity. In both, what seems like an edge is the deepest archive of memory. The living boundary - between organism and environment, or lineage and ecosystem - encodes the full history of adaptation.

A cyclical universe

In a cyclical universe (Big Bang → expansion → contraction → Big Crunch → new Bang), a key question is whether information from one cycle is preserved into the next. A singularity (infinite density, zero volume) is usually where known physics (GR + QM) breaks down. So, does memory of a prior cosmos survive the bounce?

In classical general relativity, a singularity is a boundary where information is destroyed. Spacetime curvature diverges, and predictability ends. By this view: each cycle begins anew, without inheritance. **Loop Quantum Cosmology (LQC) **replaces singularities with “quantum bounces.” Instead of infinite density, quantum geometry effects cause a rebound, which suggests some information could be carried through; no information truly lost. If applicable to cosmological bounces, then information is encoded holographically on the boundary and may reappear. **Ekpyrotic / cyclic models (brane collisions) **propose that our universe’s Big Bang is the result of higher-dimensional brane interactions. Here, information might be stored in the higher-dimensional bulk.

Black hole physics taught us: what seemed like information loss (Hawking radiation) is likely resolved by holography - information is scrambled but preserved. By analogy: the cosmic singularity may also preserve and re-encode information, though in a radically transformed (unreadable) way. In principle, if unitarity holds, information is not destroyed; it may be encoded across the bounce. In practice, that information is maximally scrambled (like ashes after a fire, or Hawking radiation after collapse). A new cycle would contain traces, but not in a way accessible as coherent “memories.” The “new universe” would inherit statistical imprints (entropy, fluctuations), not exact records.

A cyclical universe could be viewed as a kind of palimpsest: each cycle overwrites but leaves faint traces of the previous one. Information may survive as noise, statistical bias, or symmetry-breaking seeds. The cosmos may itself be a dissipative structure across cycles, retaining a form of non-organic “memory.”

String theory

String theory generalizes 1-dimensional strings to higher-dimensional objects called branes (short for membranes). A p-brane has p spatial dimensions (e.g., a 2-brane is like a surface, a 3-brane like our 3D space). In M-theory, our universe itself could be a 3-brane embedded in a higher-dimensional “bulk.” Branes can move and interact in the higher-dimensional bulk, and brane collisions can release enormous energy, manifesting as a Big Bang in the lower-dimensional brane world. After separation and expansion, gravity draws them back, leading to a new collision (cyclic universe).

Imagining the Big Bang as a brane collision avoids singularity; it replaces “beginning” with an interaction in higher-dimensional space. Data from one cycle might be encoded in the bulk or in brane tensions, carrying statistical imprints across collisions. The distance between branes can behave like a field driving acceleration and contraction. Possible imprints in the cosmic microwave background (non-Gaussianities, specific fluctuation patterns) and the observation of gravitational waves might be seen as signatures of brane dynamics.

Our observable 4D universe may be a “slice” of a higher-dimensional structure. Higher-dimensional brane interactions propose that our cosmos is not isolated but a dynamic surface in a larger multidimensional arena. Collisions, separations, and vibrations of branes could underlie cosmic origins, cycles, and even the transmission of information across apparent singularities. Brane interactions in higher dimensions offer an elegant way to reinterpret the Big Bang - not as a singular beginning, but as the energetic result of colliding multidimensional surfaces, with potential to encode memory across cosmic cycles.
